issues.legal_issue: A single land-development venture involving subdivision and sale of plots may constitute a business, and evidence of that activity may support treating the resulting proceeds as business income.
material_facts: The taxpayer acquired a village interest and a large area of land, developed part of the land, laid out the remaining land in plots, and sold those plots for a profit.
The tax tribunal found that the proceeds were income from business, and the High Court found evidence supporting that conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The High Court correctly upheld the finding that the proceeds from the plot sales were business income; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Even a single venture may be in the nature of trade or business. Acquiring land to develop and sell, then subdividing and developing it and selling it in parcels rather than as acquired, is dealing with the land as stock-in-trade. On a tax reference asking whether evidence supported the tribunal’s finding, the court examines whether the record supports that finding. No earlier cases are cited.

rule.if: income_tax_reference_appeal and land_acquired_for_resale and land_subdivided_and_developed and plots_sold_separately

predicates.income_tax_reference_appeal: The matter came before the court as an appeal concerning a finding made in an income-tax reference.
predicates.land_acquired_for_resale: The taxpayer acquired land with a view to developing and selling it.
predicates.land_subdivided_and_developed: The taxpayer divided the land into plots and developed the area to make it more attractive.
predicates.plots_sold_separately: The taxpayer sold the land in separate plots rather than as a single unit.

issues.definition: When a tax-reference appeal concerns land acquired for resale and the taxpayer subdivides and develops it before selling separate plots, the sale proceeds are treated as business income.

issues.legal_issue: A deduction available for expenditure on public welfare under an income-from-other-sources category cannot be used to show that proceeds from a land-development business are not business income.
material_facts: The taxpayer argued that the land acquisition and development served public welfare and relied on a deduction provision for public-welfare expenditure.

The court had found that the plot sales arose from a business venture and observed that the expenditure had been allowed; the question before it was whether the sale proceeds were properly included in assessable income.
issues.conclusion: The public-welfare expenditure provision, which concerned income from other sources, could not be relied on to show that the land-sale proceeds were not business income.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(5)(a) of the Hyderabad Income-tax Act concerned deductions for expenditure on public-welfare or utility works under the head of income from other sources. It could not be invoked to alter the classification of receipts found to arise from business. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.income_tax_reference_appeal: The matter came before the court as an appeal concerning a finding made in an income-tax reference.
predicates.business_activity_finding_at_issue: The tax authority treated the proceeds from the taxpayer’s activity as business income.
predicates.public_welfare_expenditure_claimed: The taxpayer relied on expenditure said to have been incurred for public welfare or utility.

issues.definition: When a tax-reference appeal concerns receipts found to arise from business and the taxpayer relies on public-welfare expenditure, that expenditure does not change the receipts’ classification as business income.
